newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli army denies targeting journalists.
newsitem.headline: Israeli army denies targeting journalists.

text.p: The Israeli army denied it deliberately shot and wounded five Arab photo-journalists covering clashes in the West Bank town of Hebron.

The journalists, who work for foreign news organisations, were among 16 Arabs wounded on Sunday by rubber-coated metal bullets fired by Israeli soldiers battling Palestinians armed with petrol bombs and rocks.
"An investigation showed there was no deliberate firing towards reporters and cameramen," an Israeli army communique said.

"It is against military policy to harm the media and whoever thinks the army deliberately shoots journalists slanders the Israel Defence Forces," the statement said, suggesting cameramen ask officers to direct them to "less dangerous" vantage points.

Hebron has been a scene of almost daily unrest for more than two weeks. Soldiers have wounded scores of Arabs in protests along a tense line dividing the Israeli and PLO-controlled parts of the city. Several soldiers have also been hurt.

Israeli soldiers shot and wounded Reuters cameraman Mazen Dana with a rubber-coated metal bullet in his shoulder while he and other journalists were filming an Israeli flag still burning after Palestinian youths had set it ablaze and fled. Dana was at home recovering after being treated at hospital.
A cameraman from Abu Dhabi was hit in the head with a rubber-coated metal bullet and seriously hurt, witnesses said.

Soldiers also shot and wounded a cameraman working for the U.S. television network ABC and one from the Associated Press. An Associated Press photographer was also hit with a rubber-coated metal bullet.
On Friday, Reuters photographer Rula Halawani was hit by a rubber bullet in the leg.

"Our attitude right now is clearly to protest to the authorities to allow us to cover the events as we should and not make journalists working in the field a target," Vice-Chairman Conny Mus of the Foreign Press Association told Reuters.
Mus said it was "very clear the soldiers are not very happy with the camera people, especially the Palestinian camera people -- and I can't see this as a coincidence any more".
Clashes also erupted on Sunday near a Jewish shrine on the outskirts of Palestinian-ruled Bethlehem in the West Bank. No serious injuries were reported.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said at the weekly cabinet meeting that Israel's aim was "to prevent a deterioration but if there will be a deterioration on the other side, it will have a very high price".
Outside Netanyahu's office, dozens of Jewish settlers demanded firmer action against Palestinian protesters in Hebron.
"The Arabs will not defeat us in Hebron. The Jewish people will win," said Noam Arnon, a spokesman for the 400 settlers in the town of 100,000 Palestinians.
"The Jews in Hebron will not be quiet. If today's hint and this demonstration are not sufficient, things will get out of hand," Arnon told the crowd in Jerusalem.
In Amman, Palestinian peace negotiator Nabil Shaath said a halt to a Jewish settlement drive in the West Bank was necessary to revive Israeli-Palestinian talks.
Formal negotiations have been frozen since Israel Strip and the West Bank, could also pave the way for resumption of talks.broke ground on a settlement in Arab East Jerusalem in March.
